writeup.headline: Ward 1 wins on the numbers you can count and loses on the ones a model guessed.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: Two of the ward's six best scores are thinner leads than a first-place finish suggests. The near-zero share of residents in an environmental-justice zone and the top mark for distance from industrial-risk sites both come from census-tract math spread evenly across each tract, so people near a tract's edge can get credited with a neighbor's numbers, and the source itself rates both figures low to medium confidence. 17 wards sit within two points of the EJ share and 27 sit within two points of the industrial-proximity score, with half the city's 50 wards packed into an 11-point band on that same measure, so first place here is a photo finish rather than a clean win. The ward's perfect participatory-budgeting score carries a different catch. It records a choice the alderman's office made about how to spend the ward's menu money, a fact about that office rather than about the neighborhood, and thirteen other wards sit inside a two-point band with that same perfect mark. The score still does real work. That participatory-budgeting vote is what funds the all-pedestrian crossing phase headed to the Milwaukee, Damen and North intersection, the project covered in this ward's recent news.
writeup.summary:
Ward 1's two best-rated categories, top coffee shops and top bars, are raw counts rather than rates, so any ward with a long stretch of commercial corridor has an edge over a ward that is mostly residential. This ward has that corridor. Block Club Chicago covered it twice in ward news this month, once for the car-free Meet Me on Milwaukee events returning across three Sundays in August, September and October, and once for a new pedestrian-only crossing phase headed to the Milwaukee, Damen and North intersection in Wicker Park. 36 top-rated coffee shops and 30 top-rated bars, both the most of any ward in the city, are the kind of count that corridor produces. 59 home-renovation permits in a single year, also a citywide high, point to the same thing from a different angle, a neighborhood still being built up rather than already finished.

Four of the ward's six weakest scores come out of the same modeling exercise, a formula built from each area's demographic mix rather than a survey of anyone who actually lives here. It puts Ward 1 dead last of the 50 wards on time poverty, expecting more residents to get under two hours of daily leisure than anywhere else in the city. The same model puts it second-to-last on total leisure minutes and ties it for third-to-last on weekly religious attendance and on how strongly residents identify with that faith. A fifth weak score, a depression rate the data does not otherwise describe, lands in that same tied slot. The one weak measure built from something countable rather than modeled is parking. The ward's residential permit-zone block faces run close to the densest in the city, a scarcity signal for anyone circling the block for a spot.

writeup.headline: Ward 2 tops the city for living alone and for trading favors with neighbors.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: The ward's best parking score is the one most likely to fool a quick read. Parking complaints make up a smaller share of all 311 activity here than in any other ward, first place on that measure. That figure is a share of total 311 activity, so it moves for two different reasons. It falls when parking complaints shrink, and it also falls when every other kind of 311 complaint grows around it, so a low share does not by itself mean parking is easy. The harder number sits among the ward's weakest scores instead. Residential permit-zone block faces here run denser than in any other ward in the city, a direct measure of competition for each spot, and it points the opposite direction from the complaint share. The ward's perfect menu-budget score deserves the same second look. It records a decision by the alderman's office about how the ward's roughly $1.5 million in annual menu money got spent, a fact about that office rather than about the neighborhood, and sixteen other wards come close enough to that same perfect mark to call it a tie.
writeup.summary:
Living alone is more common in Ward 2 than in any other ward in Chicago, just under six in ten households hold a single resident. That figure is a straight census count. The ward also ranks first for adults who trade favors with their neighbors at least monthly, and that one is a modeled estimate built on a national civic-engagement survey. The two never touch each other's data and still land in the same place. Someone without another person in the apartment has more reason to lean on whoever lives next door. The ward's worst-in-the-city rate of child-care centers is measured against total residents, and a ward this heavy with single-person households has fewer children in that population to begin with.

Two of the ward's worst scores measure the same pollution from two directions. The air-toxics hazard index and the modeled cancer-risk figure, about 33 cases per million from those same air toxics, both come from the same cumulative-impact data on the same pollutants, so a last-place finish on one predicts a last-place finish on the other rather than describing two separate problems. Winter sunlight has a simpler explanation. Ward 2's own landmark, the Olympia Centre, is a skyscraper, and Near North Side carries some of the tallest buildings in the city. Ground-level winter light reaches only about 43 percent of the ward on the solstice, second-to-last of the 50, the same shade effect that shows up wherever a ward is built mostly of towers. Street parking is scarce here for real. The ward's residential permit-zone block faces are the densest of any in the city, the kind of number that a different ranking on this page makes look like a non-issue.

writeup.headline: Ward 3's absentee-ownership number is the one ranking here that isn't part of a crowd.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: Two rankings here are easy to misread. Ward 3 ranks second in the city on a count of congregations rated 4.8 or higher with at least 25 reviews, 12 of them here, but the different measure just below it, how many distinct religious traditions those congregations represent, lands near the bottom at 47th. Highly rated and varied are different questions, and this ward only answers one of them well. The other easy misread is 48th place on menu-spending spread, how evenly the alderperson's own capital budget reaches every block instead of clustering in one corner. That number is a record of one office's spending choices rather than a fact about the neighborhood, and part of the trend behind it belongs to a ward whose lines got redrawn in 2023.
writeup.summary:
Eighty-five percent of the residential parcels in this ward list a taxpayer mailing address that isn't the property itself, the worst share of any of Chicago's fifty wards, a ranking with no caveat attached anywhere in the data. Right below it sits a related number, the share of rent that ends up as landlord profit rather than mortgage payoff, modeled two separate ways, once against each home's assessed value and once against its actual sale price. Both formulas land on 69.8 percent, the same figure to three decimal places, and both rank 47th of 50. The write-up counts that as two separate weaknesses, but it's one finding measured two different ways.

The ward's best marks split a similar way. Ward 3 places third on parks and on both 311 turnaround clocks. The parks count comes with no caveat at all, while the two 311 times carry a note that the underlying measure is not fully populated across the fifty wards. The two historic-preservation counts that look most impressive, National Register listings and official city landmarks, are ranked against smaller pools of 41 and 43 wards instead, because that data simply wasn't collected for the other nine and seven. A developer's long-delayed plan to build a grocery store, a hardware store, and new apartments on the old Stateway Gardens site would add still more units to a housing stock where 85 out of every 100 homes already answer to an owner who lives somewhere else.

writeup.headline: Ward 4 leads Chicago in landmarks, then lags on the numbers that track daily life.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: Two more rankings deserve a second look. Second place for distance to Lake Michigan sounds like a near-monopoly on the shoreline, but seven wards land within two points of Ward 4 on this measure, so it's one of several wards sitting close to the water rather than a clear runner-up. Second place on menu-budget use, the alderperson committing the full annual capital allotment rather than leaving money on the table, carries the same crowding problem, with sixteen wards inside two points of this score. That number is also a record of one office's choices rather than a fact about the neighborhood, and part of the trend behind it belongs to a ward whose boundaries changed in the 2023 redraw.
writeup.summary:
Three of Ward 4's best marks are just different ways of counting structures. It has more mapped landmarks than any other ward, 130 of them, and more mapped civic, cultural, and public places too, 212, both first in the city. A separate 1983-to-1995 survey of significant buildings built before 1940 counts 755 of them here, the second-highest total in the fifty. The landmark count and the places-of-interest count don't carry equal weight, though. The middle half of all fifty wards falls inside a tight six-point band on landmark count, so first place there is a narrow lead inside a bunched field. Places of interest spreads almost 28 points across that same middle half, so Ward 4's first-place finish on that count is a clearer, wider lead. Oakland added to that count this summer, putting up an honorary street sign for a self-taught sculptor whose outdoor art installations have stood in the neighborhood since the 1990s, one more addition to a ward that already counts more mapped landmarks and public places than any other in the city.

None of that density shows up in the numbers that describe daily life here. Chain stores dominate the ward's food retail on both counts the city keeps. About six in ten food-licensed businesses belong to a chain rather than an independent owner, and stores belonging to one of the 100 largest chains nationally make up about 21 percent of the total, the second-highest share of any ward on that specific count. School attendance points the same direction. Nearly half the students at schools serving this ward, 47.6 percent, miss a tenth or more of the school year, one of the worst rates in Chicago. The two records, the most landmarks of any ward and one of the worst attendance rates, describe the same fifty blocks.

writeup.headline: Ward 5's cleanest-air and emptiest-housing rankings come from the same quiet fact.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: Two rankings here are easy to misread. The attendance score, first in the city, only counts how often the council seat was filled. Whether anything substantive happened once it was filled is a separate question, and the same office ranks 49th of 50 on non-routine bills sponsored this session, the more direct measure of legislative output. The last-place rank on housing construction investment is also weaker in position than in substance. Thirty wards fall within two points of Ward 5's score, and the whole middle half of the city sits inside a four-point band, so finishing last here mostly means landing in a crowd near the bottom rather than standing out alone at the floor.
writeup.summary:
Ward 5's six best scores split into two groups, and one of its worst rankings belongs with them. Four of the best, its modeled cancer risk from air toxics, its distance from major polluting facilities, its pollution-burden score, and its distance from Toxic Release Inventory sites, all come from the same environmental index and all land the ward in first place citywide. Hyde Park and Woodlawn grew up around the University of Chicago as residential and institutional ground rather than an industrial corridor, consistent with a ward that never accumulated the kind of major-emitter sites that pull other wards' scores down. The fifth best score follows a related logic. Only one demolition permit was issued here last year, also a first-place finish, and two of the ward's worst rankings run close to the same math in reverse. Housing construction investment came in near zero, about three thousand dollars for the year, and only an estimated one new housing unit got permitted. Almost nothing gets torn down in Ward 5, and almost nothing new goes up either.

Two more of the ward's weak rankings point at the same quiet commercial pattern. Bars and taverns per resident rank last in the city, and chain outlets make up a bigger share of local restaurants than in 48 other wards, both signs of a retail scene that isn't drawing new investment or turnover. Ald. Yancy raised almost exactly this at a South Shore press conference in July, when he and local business owners pushed the city to ease the licensing and permitting rules they say are holding back independent businesses. Housing adds a second real story on top of the empty permit count. The Sun-Times reported in June that the Obama Center's opening is pushing existing Woodlawn units toward Airbnb conversion, with affordable units disappearing according to housing advocates quoted in the piece, and nothing in Ward 5's building data shows new supply arriving to offset it. Chronic absenteeism stands apart from all of it. Just under 48 percent of students at the ward's schools missed 10 percent or more of the school year, third-worst in the city, with nothing else on this scorecard to explain why.

writeup.headline: Ward 6 has few chain stores because it has few stores of any kind.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: A few of Ward 6's best rankings deserve a second look before anyone reads them as a boast. Three of the six best, on religious attendance, daily leisure time, and time poverty, were never measured inside the ward at all. They come from a national model built on demographic and circumstantial data rather than a local survey, and the group behind the model rates all three low confidence here. That's one modeled profile showing up three times under three separate labels. The parks-spending ranking needs a different kind of caution. Ward 6 tops the city in the share of aldermanic menu money spent on parks, near 44 percent, but that reflects one budget choice by the current officeholder rather than how many parks the ward has or how well they're kept.
writeup.summary:
Ward 6's best score and one of its worst describe the same market from two sides. Just 1.54 percent of its licensed food stores belong to one of the country's largest chains, the lowest share of any ward in Chicago. Table-service restaurants run at 1.65 per 10,000 residents, second-fewest in the city. Chains tend to open where a market already looks proven, so a ward this thin on restaurants overall will end up thin on chains too. Reporting this June backs up that picture. A Walgreens closure near 79th Street pushed the city toward a pilot program for independent pharmacies, another sign of chains pulling back rather than being crowded out by local competition.

The rest of the scorecard splits in a direction the retail story doesn't explain. Violent crime here runs at roughly 709 incidents per 10,000 residents, the worst rate of the fifty wards, and traffic injuries and the social-cohesion index both sit near the bottom too. Two more of the worst rankings, the lowest share of homes speaking a language other than English and the lowest variety of home languages spoken, draw from the same underlying share and will always move together. Building permits offer a plainer strength on their own. The city processes them here in about six and a half days, the second-fastest turnaround among the 47 wards this measure covers.

writeup.headline: Ward 7's top rankings share the podium with peers, but its worst rankings stand alone.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: The restaurant ranking is the one most likely to mislead. Ward 7 finishes 50th out of 50, but the count behind it comes from ZIP code areas rather than ward boundaries, cut however the ZIP lines happen to fall, and the source itself calls the result low confidence. It measures a rough retail footprint for that patch of the city more than an exact count within Ward 7's own lines. Packaged liquor licenses and the major chain restaurant share carry a different problem. Both come from a ward field the city recorded before the 2023 remap, so part of what's being counted still reflects the ward's old shape. All three numbers probably point the same direction, that Ward 7 has very little retail food and drink activity, but the exact rank each lands on is shakier than the number implies.
writeup.summary:
Ward 7's six best rankings are less singular than 'first in the city' sounds. Take traffic proximity, the No. 1 spot on the Chicago Environmental Justice Index, which measures nearby annual traffic volume. Four other wards finish inside two points of it. The same pattern holds across the rest of the ward's top six, the other pollution-exposure measures and the cheap rent that rounds out the list, each with three to five other wards bunched close behind. A gap that small usually means several wards are effectively tied for the top spot.

The worst six rankings tell a different story about company. Four of them, including long commutes and packaged liquor licenses, have exactly one other ward within two points of Ward 7's score, the tightest margin the site tracks. One more has two. Only the restaurant count keeps closer company, with three other wards nearby. The long commute figure puts 41 percent of workers here on the road 45 minutes or more each way, the highest share in the city, and only one other ward comes close. Mostly, Ward 7 sits alone at the bottom of a curve the rest of the city clears easily.

writeup.headline: Same few facts, counted several times, make up most of Ward 8's best and worst rankings.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: Two rankings are worth a second look. The restaurant count puts Ward 8 at 47th, a rate of 2.15 per 10,000 residents, but twelve other wards are packed within two points of that ranking, and the count itself comes from ZIP code areas rather than ward lines, rated low confidence by its own source. Whatever gap actually separates Ward 8 from its neighbors here, the 47th-place rank overstates it. The modeled certainty-of-God figure runs the other way. The number is precise, 73.9 percent, and the rank is a clean first, but no one in Ward 8 was actually asked. The estimate comes from a model trained on survey respondents elsewhere with similar demographics, projected onto this ward, and its own publisher rates it low confidence too.
writeup.summary:
Three of Ward 8's six worst rankings measure the same absence of coffee. Licensed coffee and tea shops finish 50th in the city's business-license data. A separate Google Maps sweep puts the total shop count and the highly rated subset of it at 49th. Both sources flag their own numbers as thinner than the ranks suggest, with five other wards within two points of the license count and eleven within two points of the Google Maps count. Two more of the worst six describe one fact about language rather than two. A ward with few non-English speakers will score low on any measure of language variety almost by definition, and Ward 8's multilingual and linguistic-diversity scores, both from the same Census survey, land within a point of each other at 49th.

The best six rankings repeat the same pattern, with sturdier sourcing on one pair. Child care shows up twice, once from federal business data and once from the city's own license records, two sources landing on the same conclusion. The other two strongest measures, modeled shares of adults certain God exists and calling their faith strong, come from one statistical model built on the ward's demographics rather than from anyone actually surveyed, and both call themselves low confidence. The clearest number attached to Ward 8 this year sits outside this scorecard entirely. Block Club Chicago reported in July that the ward had more than 580 open tree-cleanup requests after June's storms, the largest backlog anywhere in Chicago, a real count next to a model's guess about how residents feel.

writeup.reading_the_rankings: Take the No. 1 rank in child care centers per resident first. That count is built from ZIP code boundaries rather than ward lines, two maps that do not line up anywhere in the city, and the source rates its own confidence on this figure low. The worst-in-the-city mark for wastewater proximity looks like the sharpest possible warning, yet the measure behind it bunches almost the entire city together, with just 3.2 points separating the wards sitting in the middle of the pack. A rank at the very bottom can still land close in score to wards ranked twenty or thirty spots higher. Read the childcare count as a rough estimate of the area rather than the ward, and read the wastewater rank as one ward's position inside a tight cluster rather than a standout hazard.
writeup.summary:
Four of Ward 9's six best rankings measure the same thing from different angles. A count of 92 mapped worship buildings lands in the top three citywide, alongside a modeled estimate of how often people here attend services, a modeled share of weekly attenders, and a worship-engagement score built from Google reviews of those same buildings. The two modeled numbers are demographic estimates, built from the kind of area this looks like on paper rather than from anyone surveyed here directly, and the review score is simply engagement with the buildings the first measure already found. One concentration of faith institutions in Roseland and Pullman produces four separate top-three marks, counted once, modeled twice, and reviewed once more. The other two strengths sit outside that pattern. Child care centers per resident rank first in the city, and pothole repairs close in about two and a half days, the second fastest turnaround anywhere in Chicago.

The same Google Maps sweep behind Ward 9's worship-engagement rank also produced three of its worst six scores. It counted zero bars rated 4 stars and up, only two bars or taverns of any kind, and six coffee shops in the whole ward, one commercial survey landing near the top for one category of gathering place and dead last for three others. Ward 9's own 311 system splits the same way. It closes potholes in about two and a half days, the second fastest in the city, and takes 27.1 days on tree debris cleanup, the slowest anywhere, one request system landing at opposite ends depending on what got reported. And just over 40 percent of working residents here report a commute of 45 minutes or longer, among the worst in Chicago, which fits the ward's own geography. Roseland, West Pullman, and Pullman sit along the city's southern edge, a long ride from the Loop's jobs in any direction.

writeup.headline: One environmental index ranks Ward 10 both cleanest and most exposed in the city.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: Take the No. 1 rank in park acreage per resident first. That figure divides the park acres in the ward by how many people live there, so a rank this high can come from a small population as easily as from a lot of parkland, and most of the city sits bunched into an 11-point spread on this measure regardless of who holds the top spot. The last-place rank on household income tells a different kind of story. That number comes from an income survey covering a large multi-ward area at once, so a cluster of neighboring wards score almost identically by construction, and the source itself rates the figure low confidence. Read the parks rank as a population effect as much as a park system, and read the income rank as a description of a wider corner of the city rather than Ward 10 on its own.
writeup.summary:
Most of Ward 10's best rankings trace back to one fact, this ward has a lot of land and comparatively few people on it. Park acreage per resident ranks highest in the city, and permit-parking pressure ranks lowest, and both numbers move the same way when population is the smaller term in the ratio. Divide a fixed stock of park acres or curb space by a small number of residents and the rate climbs on its own, without a single new bench getting built. Rent lands cheapest in Chicago on two different sources, a census survey and a real-time listing index, both pricing the same thin housing stock through different pipelines, one number confirmed twice rather than two separate wins. Air-toxics hazard ranks lowest in the city and traffic proximity ranks second lowest, both consistent with a lightly built, lightly trafficked corner of Chicago.

Two of the six worst scores come from the exact same index behind two of the six best. The Cumulative Impact Assessment that puts Ward 10 first in the city for air-toxics hazard and second for traffic proximity also puts it last for nearness to hazardous-waste sites and last for nearness to freight rail lines. One data source, four separate readings, open air and light traffic on one side and waste sites and rail corridors on the other, both true about the same ward at once. Third places, the mix of cafes, bars, restaurants, and gyms measured per resident, land last at 69 per 10,000 people, licensed gyms rank last on their own at well under one per 10,000, and off-street parking lots per square kilometer land last too, three measures of built commercial infrastructure that a small population should inflate rather than depress. Instead they post the worst raw rates in the city, a real shortage of that kind of development rather than a population artifact. Household income lands last on a different basis. Its own source note says the figure is apportioned from a large multi-ward area, so a run of neighboring wards score close to identical by construction.

writeup.headline: Ward 11's best mark is confirmed twice, its worst marks trace to one source.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: Two of Ward 11's extremes deserve a closer look before they carry full weight. The last-place mark on hazard-site proximity is real, and it shares a source with four of the ward's other worst marks, the same city health index apportioned from census tracts that don't respect ward lines. The middle half of Chicago's fifty wards sit within eleven points of each other on this measure, so fiftieth place isn't necessarily far from fortieth. The first-place mark on streetlight repair time, 1.48 days on average, is ranked against all fifty wards, though the data flags the measure as not fully populated everywhere, so even this finish carries an asterisk. writeup.summary:
Ward 11's clearest strength is confirmed twice, by two sources that never talked to each other. A Google Maps sweep of every restaurant in the ward counts six percent as chain outlets, first in Chicago. The city's own business license records, a completely different system, reach the same conclusion, just over five percent chain, also first. That kind of agreement is rare on this scorecard, where most rankings rest on a single source counting one way. Grocery access adds a second real strength, second best in the city on stores per resident.

The weak side is the opposite problem, one source counted five separate times. Proximity to hazardous-chemical risk sites, to major emitter facilities, to toxic-release facilities, the diesel particulate matter in the air, and the traffic volume near homes all come from the same city health department index, each one a different slice of the same industrial exposure. The ward's own geography backs it up. Halsted Street, which runs through Bridgeport, hosted Motoblot's motorcycle crowds this June, and that same month a Chicago Department of Transportation planner working on bike infrastructure was fatally struck while biking there. The sixth weak mark, houses of worship per resident, doesn't belong to that story. It comes from a different source measuring something closer to civic geography than pollution.

writeup.headline: Ward 12's governance rankings measure one office. Its fountains measure the ward itself.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: Two of Ward 12's numbers need real translation before they say anything about the neighborhood. Second place on participatory budgeting sounds like an engaged ward, but the next thirteen wards are separated from it by under two points, and the measure itself only tracks whether the current alderperson chose to open menu-money spending to a resident vote, a decision made in one office, not a habit of the people living here. The 48th-place mark on how much of that same menu budget got spent this year is the same kind of number, another record of the office's choices rather than the ward's. The 49th-place mark on mental health providers looks close to the bottom of the entire city, but twenty-two other wards come within two points of that score, and the middle half of Chicago sits inside a seven-point band on this measure. Most of the city is bunched near this same low mark, so Ward 12's rank comes mostly from crowding, not from standing apart.
writeup.summary:
Ward 12's numbers split into three separate stories rather than one. The first is about the alderperson's office. The second-place rank on participatory budgeting and the 48th-place rank on how much of the ward's menu money got spent this year are both a record of decisions made there, rather than anything residents did or experienced. The clearest neighborhood-level fact instead sits at the park level. Two of every three park fountains tested in Ward 12 came back flagged for a historically elevated lead reading, the worst share of any ward in Chicago, and the source attaches no caveat to that number.

Three in four households speak something other than English at home, third highest in Chicago, and the ward has one of the lowest shares of people living alone in the city. Both figures come from the same census survey and carry the same caveat, apportioned from tracts that don't line up with the ward boundary, so a household near the edge could technically count toward a neighboring ward instead. The third story is about what's missing nearby. Mental health providers and everyday gathering spots (cafes, bars, restaurants, and gyms) both rank near the bottom of the city, and both come from the same method, a Google Maps count of visible business listings. A category that shows up thin on that map will score low on both measures for the same mechanical reason.

Ward 13 is last for construction dollars spent on residential permits, but fifteen other wards sit within two points of that same low score, and the source behind the number rates its own confidence as medium, so this reads as one ward inside a large cluster of quiet housing markets, not a uniquely underinvested one.
writeup.summary:
Ward 13 sits second in the city for direct sunlight reaching its sidewalks, both across the year and again on the summer solstice, essentially one fact measured twice, because Clearing, Garfield Ridge, West Lawn and West Elsdon are built low, blocks of single-family housing rather than towers, so little here casts a shadow. Midway Airport also sits inside this ward. Two separate pollution measures, one an EPA model and one the city health department's own index, both land Ward 13 last in Chicago for fine particulate matter. Neither measure names a source for that pollution, so the airport is a candidate rather than an answer. What the pair does establish is that the reading survives a federal method and a city method run independently, which is more than most single rankings on this page can claim.

The ward's housing stock looks similarly still. Ward 13 logs the second-fewest demolitions of any ward, the least residential-renovation spending in the city, and the smallest surveyed stock of historic pre-1940 buildings, three different measures agreeing that not much here is being torn down, built up, or catalogued as significant. Two of the ward's better marks belong to the ward office rather than the neighborhood. The fastest garbage-cart repair turnaround in the city and a fully spent aldermanic capital budget are decisions made by staff, and Marty Quinn, who has held the seat for fifteen years, announced this summer that he will not seek reelection, so those numbers track a term now ending rather than something residents can count on automatically. A city plan announced in July would rezone the Archer Avenue corridor through Garfield Ridge and West Lawn for hundreds of new housing units, which is the kind of project that could move the ward's weakest number, the renovation-investment ranking, in the years ahead.

writeup.headline: Large households and cheap rent explain why Ward 14's housing market sits still.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: Two of the ward's numbers look like they contradict each other, and neither is solid enough to trust at face value. The second-best rank for modeled non-religious share suggests Ward 14 is one of the more religious wards in Chicago, but that figure comes from a national survey pushed down to the ward level rather than anyone actually being asked, and the group that built it rates it low confidence. The worst-in-the-city rank for religious congregations with paid staff points the opposite way, toward a shortage of churches, but that count comes from ZIP code boundaries, which do not follow ward lines at all, so some of what should count toward Ward 14 may be filed under a neighboring ZIP instead. Read both as weak estimates rather than a real disagreement about how religious this ward is.
writeup.summary:
Ward 14 has the highest share of residents speaking a language other than English at home of any ward in Chicago, and the second-lowest share of adults living alone, so more people share a home here than in nearly every other ward. Median rent for renters paying cash is the third-cheapest in the city. Those three numbers describe one household pattern rather than three separate stories, a ward of larger, likely multigenerational households paying comparatively little for housing. That same low-turnover housing market shows up on the other end of the scorecard. Ward 14 records the fewest residential renovation permits of any ward, six issued in the tracked year, and the lowest dollar total of recorded property sales in Chicago, under seventeen million dollars. A housing market where people share space and stay in place will naturally produce fewer permits and fewer sales than one where units turn over every few years, which offers one explanation for why this ward lands last on both measures.

Air quality tells two different stories depending on which kind gets measured. Ground-level ozone, a broad regional pollutant, ranks fifth-best in the city, while proximity to facilities that report releasing toxic chemicals ranks worst of all fifty wards. Ozone drifts across the whole region and does not distinguish one block from the next, but the toxic-release measure is about specific industrial sites nearby, so the two numbers are not measuring the same thing. Amazon began demolishing the old Central Steel and Wire plant in Gage Park this spring to build a delivery station on the site, and that kind of industrial parcel is exactly what drives the proximity score. Two smaller measures, the count of massage and bodywork businesses and an unlabeled overall place-rating score, also land last, but both come from thin categories where a handful of listings decide the whole ranking. Read those as a data gap rather than a finding about the ward.

writeup.headline: Ward 15's paperwork ranks near the top, direct reads on residents sit at the bottom.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: The easiest ranking to misread is second in bills sponsored, 206 in the current council session. It reads like an active advocate winning things for the ward, but the source's own footnote calls this a record of the officeholder's choices, not a condition on the ground, and it carries the same 2023 boundary caveat as the business-license numbers next to it. It supports a claim about how one Council office operates, not about anything a resident would notice on their block. The other likely misread sits at the bottom, 0 percent of adults trading favors with neighbors and 0 percent talking to them monthly. Read on its own, that says nobody here knows their neighbor. Both numbers come from the same modeled national survey, a source that rates its own confidence low, so the honest read is that Ward 15 sits at the floor of that model relative to other wards rather than that a headcount found zero conversations on any block. The floor is still the floor. Nothing on this page argues that social connection here is strong. These two numbers just cannot be the evidence either way.
writeup.summary:
Four of Ward 15's six best rankings really describe just two things. The 19.05 percent chain-restaurant share and 1.79 percent chain-store share both come from the same business-license file, a source that rates itself medium confidence and still carries a ward boundary that changed in 2023. Both numbers say the same thing, independent owners hold the storefronts here. The 206 bills sponsored and the 37.6 percent of menu money spent on lighting share a different footnote. Both are choices made by whoever holds the Council seat, not conditions of New City, Gage Park, West Englewood, or Chicago Lawn.

Two rankings are about the ward itself, not an office or a database. A 4.65 median coffee rating, second-best in the city, and a landlord profit share of 21.5 percent, the fourth-lowest, mean less of what a renter pays here turns into pure margin over the building's assessed value. The weakest six split the same way. An estimated 0 percent of adults trade favors with neighbors and 0 percent talk to them monthly, both pulled from the same low-confidence national model, one weak read on isolation counted twice. What's left is a ward with among the highest rates of physical inactivity in Chicago, 37.5 percent of adults reporting none, one of the lowest turnout rates in the city at 22.4 percent, the smallest ride-share total of any ward at $4.46 million, and the second-smallest total of recorded property sales at $21.4 million.

writeup.headline: Every one of Ward 16's six weakest measures is the single worst of the fifty.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: The easiest number to misread is the zero-day permit average, first in the city. It sounds like an efficient building department, but the ranking only judges 47 of the fifty wards because three don't have enough recorded permits to score, and the source itself calls the figure medium confidence, so a true zero more likely means a handful of permits cleared fast than a department outpacing the rest of Chicago. Two 2026 projects, a sculpture garden opened on formerly vacant lots and a $6.4 million retail development planned for 59th Street, are exactly the kind of new construction that would start filling out that thin permit count. The other likely misread is the $1,460 asking rent, second-lowest in the city and counted as a strength on this scorecard's affordability axis. Read alone, that looks like a housing bargain. Read next to a ward that is last of fifty on health, isolation, and whether life feels exciting, the more honest explanation is that rents are low because demand is low, not because the ward is a deal.
writeup.summary:
Every one of Ward 16's six weakest rankings lands in the same place, dead last, with no ward in the city scoring worse on any of the six. Three of those six, 34.9 percent of adults in fair or poor general health, 38.2 percent reporting no leisure-time physical activity, and 63.3 percent estimated to have needed emotional support, all come from the same CDC health survey pushed from census tract down to ward level by land area. Where a tract straddles the ward line, part of what's counted here really belongs to a neighboring ward, so that's one weak health reading landing three times. What's left is the ward's own election record, a 21 percent turnout, the lowest of the fifty and an actual ballot count rather than a model. Two more numbers are modeled only, a 38.9 percent isolation figure whose source isn't even named in the data, and a 34.3 percent share expected to call life exciting rather than routine, a figure the source itself rates low confidence.

One strength carries no asterisk. None of the Park District fountains tested in the ward turned up an elevated lead reading, the cleanest result in the fifty-ward comparison. The rest complicate the picture rather than balancing it. The same style of low-confidence demographic model that puts Ward 16 last in the city on whether life feels exciting also puts it third-highest on daily leisure time, 331 minutes a day, and third-lowest on time poverty, 17.8 percent, so on paper this ward has plenty of free time and, by a different model, nothing exciting to do with it. Rent runs second-lowest in the city at $1,460 a month, a favorable mark on this scorecard's affordability measure, but next to six dead-last readings on health and connection, cheap rent here reads more like weak demand than a find.

writeup.headline: Ward 17's clearest strength is its churches, and its clearest weakness is absenteeism.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: The number a resident is likeliest to feel good about is time poverty. Ward 17 ranks second in the city here, with 17.7 percent of adults predicted to get under two hours of free time a day, a figure built from a national time-use model applied to local demographics rather than a survey taken here. The group that built it rates its own confidence low, the same rating attached to the tract-based estimate that puts civic engagement dead last a few rows down. Read together, the ward's best score and one of its worst both describe a statistical model rather than a resident's actual week, so neither is strong evidence about how life here really feels.
writeup.summary:
Two of Ward 17's best numbers describe the same fact from two directions. Ninety-six mapped houses of worship put it second in the city on a straight count, and the ward finishes second again once that count is divided by population, so scale and rate agree instead of telling separate stories. The other strength at the top, 97 percent council attendance, is a record that belongs to the alderman's office rather than to the people living here. Two service numbers land in the top three as well. Pothole repairs close in about four days, third-fastest in the city, and the citywide range on that measure is wide enough for third place to mean something real. Park acreage per resident also ranks third, but the middle of the city bunches inside an eleven-point band on that one, so third here means keeping pace with a tight pack rather than pulling ahead of it.

The six last-place finishes split into three different kinds of number. Three of them, civic engagement, short sleep, and the share of workers who walk or bike to their jobs, share one method, Census tract totals divided onto ward boundaries by area on the assumption that everyone inside a tract is spread out evenly. That method can shift a figure at the edges, but it cannot invent one. Fewer than one worker in a hundred walks or bikes to a job here, and no redraw of tract lines turns that into a middling number. Two more, mental health providers and liquor-licensed restaurants, are counted directly through real licenses and listings, and each lands inside a crowd. On providers, twenty-two wards are packed inside a two-point band with Ward 17 at the bottom of it, which makes the shortage a citywide one that this ward sits at the worst end of. Liquor-licensed restaurants repeat the pattern on a smaller scale, eleven wards bunched together at the floor. Chronic absenteeism stands apart from both groups. No other ward comes close to Ward 17's score here, and 52 percent of students at ward schools missed at least a tenth of the school year, the one number on this list with nothing else nearby.

writeup.headline: Almost no retail exists in Ward 18, and its high car ownership is the evidence.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: Two rankings are easy to misread as achievements or failures unique to Ward 18, and neither is what it looks like. The alderman's office spent almost all of the ward's roughly $1.5 million annual capital allotment last year, good for fourth in the city, but that is a record of the officeholder choosing to commit the money, not a condition of the ward itself. Sixteen wards cluster inside two points of Ward 18's own score here, nearly a third of the city spending its allotment at essentially the same clip, so fourth place means keeping pace with the pack rather than standing out from it. Entertainment venues sit at the very bottom for a different reason. Licensed theaters, music halls and event spaces are rare enough across all fifty wards that the middle of the field spans only about ten points and 16 wards bunch within two points of each other, meaning Ward 18's last-place finish here describes a citywide amenity that barely exists anywhere rather than a gap specific to this ward.
writeup.summary:
Line up Ward 18's business-license counts and one fact explains most of the page. The ward ranks first in the city for having the fewest licensed tobacco retailers per resident, and it ranks dead last for licensed grocery stores, licensed entertainment venues, and both of the coffee-shop quality counts this project tracks. The 4.5-star bar and the easier 4-star bar turn up the same result, zero qualifying coffee shops here. All five numbers measure the same thing, how much retail exists in the ward, and the direction just depends on whether the retail type being counted is something residents want more of or less of. Fewer tobacco shops reads as a win. Fewer groceries, fewer places to sit with a drink, and no coffee shop that clears either quality bar all read as losses, but underneath, it is one ward with very little commercial activity of any kind.

Two more strengths describe the housing itself rather than the retail around it. Ward 18 also ranks first in the city for owner-occupancy, tracked by how often a home's tax bill goes to the same address as the property, though the underlying share is just 45.79 percent absentee-owned, meaning every other ward in Chicago does even worse on this measure. Only one demolition permit was issued in the ward's most recent full year, third-fewest citywide, another sign of a settled, low-turnover housing stock. The retail gap shows up again in car ownership. Vehicles per household rank 49th of 50, and because this measure scores fewer cars as the good outcome, 49th means close to the opposite of what the rank number suggests, one of the highest counts in the city, 1.7 vehicles per household, which is what you would expect where the nearest grocery store or coffee shop means a drive. Rent burden stands apart from everything above. Sixty-three percent of renter households here spend 30 percent or more of income on rent, the worst share of the fifty wards, with no other ward inside two points of it. That number points the opposite direction from a housing stock that otherwise looks settled and owner-held.

writeup.headline: Ward 19's best and worst numbers share one cause, low density built around cars.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: Two of Ward 19's first-place rankings look like verdicts on how residents feel, though neither is measuring that directly. The modeled share of adults satisfied with their finances tops the city at 33.7 percent, and the modeled share afraid to walk alone at night is lowest in the city at 39.1 percent. First place on both means the ward's demographic profile scored better than the other forty-nine wards' profiles in the same model, a relative rank rather than a report from anyone who lives here. Both figures are modeled from demographics rather than counted from a survey taken in the ward, and the same source rates its own reliability low. The pedestrian and cyclist crash count invites a similar correction. Ranking first with 21 crashes reads as the safest streets in the city, but the ward also has the third-lowest share of workers who commute by transit and few people out walking or biking to begin with. One of the ward's speed cameras, its lowest-ticketing, sits on 99th Street and may move to a stretch near two schools on 111th Street after parents there raised safety concerns, hardly the sign of a ward that treats its top ranking here as a settled score.
writeup.summary:
Ward 19 has the fewest pedestrian and cyclist crashes of the fifty wards, a raw count of 21, and also the third-lowest share of workers who commute by transit, 9.2 percent. Those numbers describe the same place. Few residents are out walking, biking or riding transit, so few end up struck doing it. Grocery stores per resident and licensed entertainment venues sit in the same low range, 1.03 per 10,000 residents and 49th of fifty for venues, a retail count that follows the housing pattern in this low-density stretch of the far southwest side. The businesses that do exist can still draw a crowd. The Original Rainbow Cone just marked its 100th year on Western Avenue, and Horse Thief Hollow's barrel-aged beer won gold at a national competition, proof that a thin venue count reflects density more than quality.

Voter turnout is a cleaner win, 62 percent of registered voters, the highest share in the city and a straight count rather than a model. The alderman put 99.6 percent of this year's menu money into street resurfacing, also the most of any ward, and that same decision produces the ward's dead-last score for menu spending diversity. A budget concentrated almost entirely in one category cannot also score high on variety. Both numbers come from the same choice.

writeup.headline: City services rank high in Ward 20 while every measure of money sits at the bottom.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: The number to distrust most is the one that looks best. First place for socializing with neighbors weekly comes from the same demographic model that puts the ward last on happiness and 49th of 50 on trust, and its publisher rates it low confidence. A model that produces both extremes for one ward is describing its own inputs rather than the neighborhood. The street-resurfacing figure needs a different caution. It records how the ward office chose to spend its repair budget, a decision by an officeholder rather than a condition on the ground, and committing nearly all of a year's budget to one category says as much about the state of the streets as about anyone's priorities.
writeup.summary:
The split in this ward's numbers is the story. Garbage carts get serviced sixth-fastest in the city, permit-parking pressure is among the lowest, nearly all of the ward's street budget went into repaving, and new housing permits run sixth-highest. Then every measure of private money lands at the floor. More than a third of residents live below the poverty line, the worst rate of the fifty, and household income is second-lowest. On this scorecard the city's basic services are holding up here. The gap is in what residents earn.

Four of the ward's six worst rankings are modeled estimates of happiness, satisfaction and trust, built from demographics rather than from asking anyone who lives here. Those four are largely the poverty rate wearing different labels and should be read as one finding rather than four. This is also the quarter to write the baseline down. With the Obama Center opening nearby and the Woodlawn Central development approved, the poverty, income and permit lines on this page are the ones that will show whether any of that investment reaches the people already living here.

writeup.headline: Ward 21 funds schools and streets well and has almost no bars or liquor licenses.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: The ranking most likely to get misread is the liquor-license count, 49th in the city. The gap behind it is not close to what the rank implies. Twelve wards finish inside two points of Ward 21 here, so 49th describes a crowded tie rather than a ward standing out as uniquely dry. The zero count of top-rated bars reads as a cleaner story, a straight count rather than a model, though eight other wards are within two points of it, so the floor here is crowded. Read next to the highest chain-restaurant share in the city, the two rankings describe the same absence of an independent dining and drinking strip rather than two different problems.
writeup.summary:
Three of Ward 21's six best rankings, for weekly religious attendance, overall religious attendance, and strength of religious affiliation, are one signal counted three times rather than three separate wins. All three come from the same demographic model rather than a count of anyone in the ward, so once the ward's makeup produces one high modeled score, the other two follow along for free. The genuinely independent strength sits one spot down. Per-pupil school spending ranks second in the city at $23,247 a student, a reported figure rather than a model. The alderman backs that up on the street budget, putting 97.3 percent of this year's menu money into resurfacing, third most of any ward, though the same choice is why alley spending and menu diversity both rank near the bottom. Money concentrated almost entirely on streets cannot also spread across alleys and other categories.

None of that public investment shows up on the ward's commercial strip. Ward 21 has the highest share of chain restaurants in the city, 35 percent, no bars rated 4.5 stars or better with at least 50 reviews, and one of the lowest counts of restaurants licensed to pour liquor. In May, a $20 million state grant revived a program rehabbing and reselling 33 vacant homes across Roseland and Englewood, and Roseland is one of this ward's four neighborhoods. writeup.headline: Ward 22's only two caveat-free numbers both track landlord profit, and they agree.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: The camera-spending ranking at first place is the one to read most carefully. It records a spending choice the current alderperson made with a discretionary aldermanic fund, not a condition of the neighborhood, and the middle half of the city's fifty wards, roughly 13th through 38th place, span zero points on this measure, so the first-place finish sits inside a pile of wards bunched at the same value rather than clear of the field. The perfect 5.0 coffee rating carries a quieter version of the same problem. This metric isn't measured in every ward, so the ranking compares Ward 22 only against the wards where a rating exists, not against all fifty, which makes a rating that looks flawless less remarkable than the number one spot suggests.
writeup.summary:
Ten of the twelve measures featured on this page carry at least one caveat, a flag about how the number was built or how far to trust it. The two that carry none are both about landlord profit, one using a rental unit's assessed value as the mortgage basis and one using its last sale price, and both rank 2nd best in Chicago. Different mortgage basis, same math, one finding stated two ways. Renters here hand over less of their rent as landlord profit than almost anywhere else in the city, and it is the rare number on this page worth taking at face value.

The worst numbers work the opposite way. Two measures of how often adults trade favors with neighbors or talk to them tie for the literal bottom of the city, and both land at 0.0 percent, built by blending a civic engagement survey with census data and flagged low confidence by the source itself. Taken literally, that would mean no adult in the ward reports even a monthly chat with a neighbor, an implausible headcount for any inhabited area, so the tie reads as a model running out of range rather than a finding about how the ward actually socializes. The environmental numbers split in a similar way, and this is where counting caveats stops being the point. Ozone ranks 2nd best in the city, while the broader Environmental Justice index and a toxic-release measure both rank 49th. Ozone drifts in across the whole region. The other two are built around what sits nearby, and a near-bottom finish on both is not something one clean pollutant reading offsets. The 216 resident surveys behind Garfield Ridge's new community plan are the kind of ground-level count the modeled neighbor numbers don't have.

writeup.headline: Ward 23's fullest households and its heaviest car ownership are one fact stated twice.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: Two of the ward's six last-place finishes are softer than they look. The measure labeled review_count ties Ward 23 to the bottom of the city at a value of 1,070, but 36 of the 50 wards land within two points of that same score, so this last place stands on a difference that barely exists, closer to a rounding error than a real gap. The last-place finish for weekly bar visits comes from a demographic model rather than a survey of who actually went to a bar, and the source itself calls it low confidence, so it says more about wards shaped like this one on paper than about anyone's Friday night. Parks, civic and cultural places, and cars per household don't have that problem. All three are direct counts with no caveat attached, and all three land Ward 23 at the true bottom of the city.
writeup.summary:
Ward 23 ranks first in Chicago for the lowest share of one-person households, meaning shared and family households are more common here than in any other ward. It also ranks last for cars per household, the highest average vehicle count of any ward. Those two rankings are close to the same fact. A home holding more residents holds more potential drivers, so a ward built around larger households will naturally carry more cars per household than one full of people living alone, without any transit failure or car culture needed to explain the gap.

A second signal shows up in how little of this ward is public space. It ranks last in Chicago for mapped parks, with just 4 inside its boundaries, and last for civic and cultural places, with 18 mapped total, and neither number carries a caveat the way most of this page's rankings do. The ward's most visible piece of civic life is a single Garfield Ridge senior center marking 30 years of service, the kind of load one building carries in a ward this thin on mapped gathering space. The 800 new housing units planned for the Archer Avenue corridor will add residents to a ward that already ranks last on parks and places before a single unit is built.

writeup.headline: Ward 24 tops Chicago in churches and school funding, and ranks worst on pollution.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: Two of these rankings deserve a second look before taking them at face value. The 1st-place rank for grocery stores per resident comes from a source that counts businesses by ZIP code, and ZIP codes don't follow ward lines, so some of that count may really belong to a store just over the boundary in a neighboring ward, and the source itself rates the measure low confidence. The 2nd-place rank for evenings spent with neighbors and the 50th-place rank for trust in those same neighbors look like they contradict each other, and in a sense they do, but both come from one statistical model, run on the same demographic inputs, describing what a ward shaped like this one usually looks like rather than anything counted or asked of an actual Ward 24 resident. Read as two predictions from a single formula instead of two separate community facts, and the contradiction becomes a property of the model rather than a mystery about the neighborhood.
writeup.summary:
Chicago draws its fifty wards to hold roughly the same number of residents, so a ward that leads the city on the raw count of something almost always leads on the per-capita version of it too. Ward 24's 101 mapped faith institutions and its top rank for worship places per resident are the same fact counted two ways. The ward also spends more per student than any other school system in the city, $23,663, and ranks first for grocery access. Those numbers describe what got built here. A different kind of number describes something else. A statistical model built from the ward's demographic makeup predicts more evenings spent with neighbors here than in almost any other ward in Chicago, and the same model, fed the same inputs, predicts the least trust in those neighbors of anywhere in the city. Neither number comes from asking a resident anything. They are two outputs of one formula, and the formula disagrees with itself.

The ward's worst numbers cluster the same way its best ones do. Its score on the city's environmental justice index and its share of residents living inside an EJ-designated area are drawn from the same pollution assessment, so a worst-in-the-city rank on one all but guarantees a worst-in-the-city rank on the other, and Ward 24 has both. That pattern holds up even without the demographic model behind it. Two of the ward's other bottom rankings start from health surveys that ask residents directly, then get spread across census tracts to reach the ward line. The share of adults reporting frequent mental distress is the highest of any ward in Chicago, and the share who say they feel part of their neighborhood is the lowest. New construction is landing on that same baseline right now. The city broke ground this summer on nine three-flats in North Lawndale, 27 units total, and the council approved a six-story, 59-unit building on a nearby vacant lot, both inside the ward the pollution data ranks worst in Chicago.

writeup.headline: Ward 25 tests cleanest for regional air and near worst for closeness to heavy industry.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: Two of the ward's strongest-looking numbers reward a closer look. Third place for menu money spent on schools sounds like a real commitment, but the ward's own share is just 3.5 percent, and nearly every ward in Chicago is packed into that same narrow band, so third place separates almost nothing from fiftieth. Third place for participatory budgeting reads the same way. More than a dozen other wards land close enough in score to call it a tie, which makes giving residents a vote on menu money look like standard practice across Chicago rather than something this ward stands out for. Neither ranking is wrong. Both are measuring differences too small for the ordinal number to carry much meaning.
writeup.summary:
The city's environmental justice index is built from several separate measures, and for this ward they point in different directions. Ozone, a measure of regional ground-level air quality, ranks best in Chicago here. Proximity to major industrial emitters ranks 48th, and the index's own pollution-burden score ranks 47th, both near the bottom. All three numbers come from the same city assessment. Ozone drifts across a whole region and rarely tracks one neighborhood's industry, while a proximity score is built to measure exactly that, and this ward has industry to be near. The city opened a planning study this spring of Pilsen's industrial corridor, a stretch of roughly 1,000 acres of factories and rail lines inside the ward, which is precisely what a proximity or burden score is built to register, even while the air above the whole area tests clean.

A second split runs through the ward's money, and it traces back to the officeholder rather than the neighborhood. More than half of this term's aldermanic menu money went to alley repair, one of the highest shares in the city, while street resurfacing got the smallest share of any ward, 3.2 percent. Both numbers record a choice made with one discretionary pot of cash. Five people are already running for the seat that makes that choice, and the current alderman hasn't said if he wants another term. One number here traces to neither money nor industry. Chronic school absenteeism, just under half of students missing 10 percent or more of the school year, is the second worst rate in Chicago, and nothing else on this page explains it.

writeup.headline: Ward 26's independent businesses lead the city while its street repairs lag it most.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: Two rankings here look worse than they are. Menu budget utilization reads like an underspent account because it sits near the bottom of the city's ranking, but the ward actually committed 85.3 percent of its roughly $1.5 million yearly allotment to projects, real follow-through that ranks low only because most other wards spent an even higher share of theirs. Yoga and pilates studios read the opposite way. Ward 26 sits near the bottom of that ranking with zero studios per 10,000 residents, but a two-point spread covers fifteen other wards at that same number, close to a third of the city bunched at the same floor, so the rank implies the ward stands out for an absence that is actually common.
writeup.summary:
Ward 26's strongest rankings all describe the same kind of neighborhood, one where people spend money at places somebody nearby actually owns. Independent restaurants outnumber chains here more than in any other ward, independents hold a bigger share of the licensed food stores than in all but one other ward, and the ward's houses of worship rate second-highest in Chicago on Google. Its bars rate near the top too, among the wards with enough listed to compare. The Puerto Rican Parade returned to the Division Street corridor this summer, the same strip of small, individually run shops those business-license counts are describing. Those counts rest on softer ground than the repair numbers below. They come from a ward boundary that predates the 2023 redrawing, and the office that compiled them rates its own confidence as medium, so the wide lead at the top is less solid than first place implies.

The weak rankings point at streets too, but from two different directions. Two of them track the same pot of money, the roughly $1.5 million the alderperson's office spends each year on ward projects, and they pull against each other. That money is more spread out across the ward, adjusted for its size and shape, than in any other ward in Chicago, yet only 16.4 percent of it went to street resurfacing, one of the smallest shares in the city. Both numbers describe a choice made in the alderperson's office, not a condition in the neighborhood. The city's own repair queue is a separate matter, and it is the slowest anywhere. Pothole requests take more than 60 days to close, worst of the fifty, and general 311 requests average 16.3 days, second worst. How long city crews take to show up once someone calls has nothing to do with how the ward's own money gets spent.

writeup.headline: Ward 27's growth explains its building lead and its near-worst crash counts alike.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: Two numbers here deserve more scrutiny than their rank suggests. The $256.4 million in TIF increment revenue is the flashiest of the ward's firsts, but it is also the softest, built by the same team that rates its own confidence in the figure low, and the comparison covers only 49 wards, one short of the full city. The pollution-proximity ranking needs a different kind of care. Worst in the city sounds like a precise reading for any one block, and the figure is spread across census tracts on the assumption that everyone inside a tract is affected evenly, so it describes the ward as a whole rather than a given address. The sites themselves do not move with the tract lines, and Ward 27 sits closer to more of them than any other ward in Chicago.
writeup.summary:
Ward 27 leads Chicago on every measure of new building. It posted the most reported construction investment in new residential permits of any ward, at $279.7 million, and the largest estimate of new housing units on the way, at 633, with the most permits issued too. Two small businesses opened on West Town's Chicago Avenue this summer alone, a crowdfunded Basque pintxos bar and Joe Freshgoods's new store and cafe, real evidence of the same building wave the permit data describes. Arts and culture space nearly matches that lead, with 13 mapped venues, the second-most in the city. None of those numbers are a runaway victory. The gap between wards on two of the construction measures is narrow, only four or five points across the entire middle half of the city, so those firsts are a slim margin over a crowded field of wards that are also building. The raw permit count is the exception, spread almost 28 points across that same middle half, so that first place is the one with real distance behind it.

The weak rankings cluster in two different places, and both read differently once the ward's growth is the backdrop. The 607 traffic injuries and 173 pedestrian and cyclist crashes logged here both sit second-to-last in the city, but they come from the same crash log, and both are raw counts rather than rates. A ward adding this much new construction and this many new residents will log more incidents in absolute terms than a quieter one even at the same risk per person. The pollution numbers are a separate matter. Ward 27 ranks worst in the city for how close residents live to Superfund and brownfield sites, and near-worst for nearby toxic-release facilities, both pulled from the same environmental assessment. That pairing is one exposure profile read twice rather than two independent findings, and it is the part of this page the building boom does not explain.

writeup.headline: One tract method carries three of Ward 28's worst ranks and softens none of them.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: The two rankings on how often residents see friends and neighbors weekly, third and fourth in the city at 18.3 and 20.7 percent, are the ones most likely to read as real community warmth. Neither number was collected here. Both come from a model that looks at a ward's age, income, and household mix and predicts what a similar ward usually reports in national surveys, and the source itself flags the estimate as low confidence. The traffic injury count needs a different correction. A total of 902 reads like the single worst safety number in the city, and it is a raw count rather than a rate, so it climbs with how much traffic moves through the ward as well as with the risk of any one trip. That does not shrink it. It makes 902 the right number for asking how much crash response this ward absorbs and the wrong one for ranking how dangerous a given drive here is.
writeup.summary:
The most convincing of Ward 28's six best rankings are the ones nobody had to model. It has more mapped gardens than any ward in the city, 23 in total, and the fourth-highest count of civic and cultural places, 136, both pulled straight off the map rather than estimated. New residential permits add a third real count, 29 in total, also fourth-best in the city. In Austin, three families are preparing to move into Habitat for Humanity's first three homes on the West Side this summer.

The weak half of the scorecard is three separate findings that happen to arrive by one route. Poverty sits at 30.5 percent of residents. Proximity to Superfund and brownfield sites lands at the same rank, and so does the 79.3 percent of the ward inside a city-designated Environmental Justice priority area. All three are built by splitting census tracts along the ward's edge and assuming residents sit evenly across each one, which blurs where a number falls at the boundary without changing its level. Close to a third of the people here live below the poverty line under any reasonable redraw of those lines, and four fifths of the ward sits inside an EJ priority area. The same strain shows up in numbers that never touch a census tract. Traffic injuries, 902 last year, are the worst count in the city, and in July seven Save A Lot stores across the South and West Sides, including the West Garfield Park location on Pulaski, faced sudden closure over what their owners called financial headwinds. Chain restaurants make up close to half the ward's licensed restaurants, near the bottom of that ranking as well.

writeup.headline: Ward 29 has the cleanest ozone reading in Chicago and almost no gardens.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: Two of these rankings read as more decisive than the numbers behind them support. Menu money spent on surveillance cameras ranks second in the city at 0.2 percent, which sounds like a deliberate governance choice, but it is a decision by the alderman's office about ward spending, not a fact about the neighborhood, and the citywide middle band on that measure spans less than a single point. Nearly every ward reports a number this close to zero, so finishing second says less than it looks like. The garden count runs the same pattern from the bottom. Zero gardens mapped lands the ward 47th, which reads like a clear last place, but seventeen other wards are bunched inside two points of the same zero. Close to a third of the city is bunched at the foot of this list, so the real distance between Ward 29 and a typical low-garden ward is small, even though the rank makes it look large.
writeup.summary:
Ward 29's clearest strength is air quality, and it shows up twice. Two separate ozone measurements, one an EPA-modeled annual average and the other a city environmental-justice index built from summer readings, both land near the top of the city, first and seventh. The same air is being measured two different ways, and both readings agree. The ward's other real strength is how fast the city responds here. Chicago 311 closes graffiti removal requests in well under a day, the third-fastest turnaround of the fifty.

Everything about outdoor space and upkeep runs the other way. The ward has no mapped gardens, only one registered mural, and sits farther from Lake Michigan than all but a handful of other wards, a fact about where the ward sits on the map rather than anything the ward is doing wrong. Half of its park drinking fountains have tested positive for elevated lead at some point, and pothole repairs take 35 days on average, among the slowest turnarounds in the city. Parking complaints make up a larger share of local 311 activity here than in all but four other wards.

writeup.reading_the_rankings: Zero mapped libraries, second-worst in the city, is the ranking most likely to read as an amenity desert, but it is a raw count tied to a boundary that was redrawn in 2023, not a distance to the nearest branch, and a library assigned two blocks over the line would still show up here as zero. The garbage cart repair time runs the other way. Nearly twenty days to close a routine maintenance call sounds unremarkable on its own, yet it ranks fourth of the full fifty. The rank is honest and the wait is still close to three weeks, which says more about the citywide pace on this request than about anything the ward office decides.
writeup.summary:
Two of this ward's best rankings ask the same question with two different price tags and land in nearly the same place. One estimates a rental unit's mortgage-equivalent cost off the last price the property actually sold for. The other uses the property's assessed value instead. Either way, less than six percent of rent is left over as landlord profit once that modeled cost comes out, the smallest share posted by any Chicago ward on both versions. The ward's ownership pattern points the same direction without proving it. Just under 54 percent of residential parcels here have an owner whose mailing address differs from the property, which sounds high on its own, but it is the fifth-lowest share of the fifty, so most of Chicago runs higher. The two facts come from separate questions inside the same assessor and rental data, and together they describe a ward held mostly by owners with thin margins rather than portfolios built to extract them.

A similar split shows up in the ward office's own spending. The roughly $1.5 million the ward receives each year through the city's menu program landed across an unusually wide spread of blocks, second-best of the fifty wards, but only 79.2 percent of that pot got committed to projects in the latest full year, fourth-worst of the fifty. Both numbers describe the same fund and the same office rather than the neighborhood, and one says more about how the money moved than the other does about how much the ward needed. A bigger sum arrived by a different route this year. State and city officials, including Ald. Ruth Cruz, secured $13 million this summer for a shelter for older adults, close to nine times the ward's entire annual menu allotment in one grant. Whatever is holding back the last fifth of that smaller pot, it is not a shortage of the office landing money elsewhere.
