writeup.headline: Ward 31's two parking measures agree, ruling out the easy excuse for either one.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: The lowest measured exposure to polluted sites, first of fifty, is the ranking most likely to read as a clean bill of health for the ward, but the source grades its own confidence as medium, a few wards never reported a number for this measure at all, and the figure is allocated from census-tract shapes that were not built to match ward boundaries. A first-place rank here is a real signal of low industrial exposure, not a certified one. New housing tells the opposite story. A single permit pulled here last year is the fewest of any ward, but the ranking says less than the number of wards packed in right behind it. Twenty-nine other wards fall within two points of this same score, and the middle half of the fifty wards citywide sits inside a five-point band on this measure. Last place here is a real number, one permit, but it belongs to a citywide slump rather than a problem unique to this ward.
writeup.summary:
Every parking measure Ward 31 tracks lands in last place, and the two ways it gets there close off the easiest excuse for either result. One counts parking complaints against the ward's physical area. The other asks what share of everything the ward reports to 311, potholes, rodents, streetlights, all of it, is about parking specifically. A ward that simply files more 311 complaints than anywhere else could top the first measure without topping the second, since the share measure already divides by its own total volume. Ward 31 finishes last on both, so the complaints concentrate on parking itself, more than in any other ward in Chicago, rather than reflecting a ward that reports more of everything.

The ward is fast at fixing what is already there. Streetlight-outage requests close in under two days on average, one of the quickest turnarounds in the city. A planned piece of new infrastructure tells a different story. A traffic signal at Belmont and Kilbourn in Hermosa had been planned since 2023 and was still not installed this June, when a 62-year-old woman was struck and killed crossing that intersection. Keeping existing equipment running and building something that was not there yet are two different kinds of city response, and only one of them is fast here. Two more of the ward's worst rankings stand on their own rather than pairing with anything else on this page. An estimated 18.3 percent of residents carry no health insurance, the highest uninsured share of the fifty, and rodent baiting requests take longer to close here than anywhere else in the city. Neither shares a data source or a cause with the parking numbers or with each other. They are just two more places this ward finishes last.

writeup.headline: Ward 32 pairs the highest income in Chicago with the least free time to enjoy it.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: Two of the flashiest firsts here need a second look before they mean what they seem to. Population vulnerability, ranked 1st, reads like a warning, but this measure runs in reverse, a lower raw score earns a better rank, and Ward 32's number one means the city's environmental-justice index found the least at-risk population profile of any ward, not the most. The modeled-happiness ranking needs the opposite kind of correction. It reads like an independent finding, residents here are the happiest in Chicago, but the model behind it is built from the ward's income, marital status, employment, homeownership and health mix, the same inputs already covered by the income and poverty numbers above, and the source itself grades the estimate low confidence. It is closer to a second reading of the ward's wealth than a survey of how anyone here actually feels.
writeup.summary:
Every top mark in this ward comes back to the same fact, this is the most expensive corner of the city to live in. Median household income runs $166,248 a year, the highest of any ward, and the poverty rate sits at 5.9 percent, the lowest. The city's environmental-justice index scores the ward's population as the least at-risk in Chicago on the same kind of income, health and household data behind those two numbers. Even the nightlife number fits the pattern, 5.73 bars and taverns per 10,000 residents, the highest rate in the city, which is what a small, dense footprint full of paying customers produces when a ward's commercial strips get compressed into a few square miles instead of spread thin.

The weak marks price the same real estate a different way, through construction instead of dollars. Thirty-eight wrecking permits have gone out here, the most of any ward, and this year's news explains the pattern. A city commission cleared roughly $200 million in public funding for the Foundry Park project on the former Lincoln Yards site, and the City Council approved a 30-unit building on a lot in the ward that had sat vacant for years. Ground that gets torn down and rebuilt this often leaves less of it standing long enough to register as a landmark or sitting empty long enough to hold a garden, and Ward 32 counts zero of each, one rank off the bottom of the city on both. The social numbers run on a similar recipe. Weekly neighbor socializing and daily leisure time are both modeled from a ward's demographic mix and density, the same kind of inputs that produce the income and happiness numbers above, just run through a different formula and pointed the other way, worst in Chicago on both instead of best.

writeup.headline: Ward 33 rates well in the businesses people visit and lags in the services the city runs.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: One ranking here is easy to misread on its own. Total place reviews lands 49th of 50, which looks like a verdict on quality, but reviews are a raw count, and thirty-six of the fifty wards sit within two points of each other on this measure, the whole city bunched into a narrow band. The measure that actually grades what's here, average place rating at 4.73, second-best in Chicago, shows the businesses earning strong marks from the people who do visit, even with a lower volume of total visits than most of the city. The chain-store ranking deserves its own caveat. The 13.79 percent figure behind the ward's lowest-in-Chicago chain share comes from business-license records tied to whatever ward shape existed when each license was filed, and the ward's boundaries were redrawn in 2023, so part of that record describes a differently shaped ward than the one that exists today.
writeup.summary:
Nearly every strong mark in this ward measures the same thing, how good the experience is once someone shows up, and the ward's other numbers show fewer people showing up to begin with. The ward's bars carry a median Google rating of 4.75, the best of the 45 wards with rated bars, houses of worship rate 4.9, third-best, and places across the ward average 4.73 out of 5, second-best in Chicago. Total place reviews, the one number here that counts visits instead of grading them, lands 49th of 50, because a residential stretch away from downtown and its tourist traffic pulls in fewer reviewers even as the people who do stop by rate the place highly. Chain stores back up the read. Just 13.79 percent of the ward's licensed food stores are chains, the lowest share in Chicago, and a July opening captured the type exactly, a family-run Uyghur restaurant on Pulaski Road in Albany Park serving home cooking rather than a franchise menu.

The weak marks run on a different clock, the city's own. Only 55.9 percent of the roughly $1.5 million the ward's office gets each year for capital projects actually went to committed work in the latest full year, worse than any other ward, a fact about how that budget got managed rather than about the neighborhood itself. The same slowness shows up where residents feel it directly. The city takes 13.94 days on average to close a 311 request here, 48th of 50, and 40.61 days to fix a pothole, also 48th. This summer's Block Club coverage caught the pattern in real time, a new riverside plaza at Ronan Park finally opened after residents had waited long enough for it to be called 'long-awaited' in the headline, and the ribbon-cutting itself was overtaken by dueling protests over a homeless encampment nearby. No library location and only one registered mural turn up inside the ward's boundary in this dataset, both among the lowest counts in the city, one more sign that whatever gets built or logged here does so slowly.

writeup.headline: Ward 34's rankings measure a business core's daytime crowd more than its residents.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: Two of Ward 34's numbers look contradictory before you check what each one actually measures. The ward ranks first in the city for religious congregations with paid staff, 7.09 per 10,000 residents, yet finishes last on a modeled estimate that puts 38.48 percent of adults here as having no religious affiliation. The congregation count comes from a business-registry source that spreads county-level counts across ZIP codes rather than the ward's actual boundary, so it counts staffed offices more than it counts where worshippers actually live, the same daytime-crowd pattern behind the ward's other firsts. The no-affiliation figure is a demographic model built from citywide survey patterns rather than a count of anyone's belief, and the source rates it low confidence on its own. Ward 34's last-place finish on landlord profit share deserves the same second look. Ten other wards fall inside two points of the same estimate on both the assessed-value and sale-price versions, so the ward sits at the extreme edge of a citywide cluster rather than standing alone at the bottom.
writeup.summary:
The Loop sits inside this ward, so the denominator under most of Ward 34's rates is a resident count far smaller than the weekday crowd on its streets. Six of its strongest marks trace back to that gap. Bank branches run 23.95 per 10,000 residents here, the most of any ward, and coffee shops, gyms, licensed coffee and tea shops, and religious congregations all rank first by the same per-resident math. The 'L' logged more than 7.4 million entries at stations inside the ward last year, the highest of the 36 wards this measure covers, a count that tracks commuters and downtown crowds far more than the people who actually sleep here. That same thin denominator shows up on the worst side of the ledger too. Tobacco retailers run 16.61 per 10,000 residents here, more than in any other ward, and Ward 34 also carries the heaviest traffic exposure of any ward, an index score of 3,403.7. Both numbers measure activity that a small resident count cannot explain by itself.

A second, separate signal runs through the numbers, and it is about money rather than headcount. Ward 34 finishes last in the city on the estimated share of rent that ends up as landlord profit, above 69.8 percent under both the assessed-value and sale-price versions of that estimate. It also posts the highest share of food stores belonging to one of the 100 largest retail chains in the country, 24.36 percent, the most chain-heavy food retail of any ward in Chicago. writeup.headline: Ward 35's independent dining strip has some of the city's least park and gathering space.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: Ward 35's 49th-place finish on 'beloved congregations' is the number most likely to read as a verdict on the neighborhood's faith or community life. The measure only counts worship places with a Google rating of 4.8 or higher and at least 25 reviews, a bar most congregations never clear regardless of their size or quality, since it depends on parishioners posting reviews online. All fifty wards are ranked on it, so the finish itself is solid. What the finish ranks is Google activity around worship places rather than worship. The alder attendance rate in the bottom five wards deserves the same caution. That figure blends more than one officeholder's term across the 2023 boundary redraw and carries only medium confidence from its own source, a fact about an office stitched across a boundary change more than a verdict on the people living here.
writeup.summary:
Only one ward in Chicago has a lower share of chain restaurants than Ward 35's 9.13 percent, and its bars post a median Google rating of 4.6, fourth-best among wards with enough rated bars to count. Those two numbers describe one commercial strip, the first counting who owns it and the second grading it. Renters here also give up less of their income to rent than in most of the city. About 35.4 percent of renter households spend 30 percent or more of their income on rent here, the fifth-lowest burden of the fifty wards. The ward's aldermanic office backs the same walkable character with money. Of the roughly $1.5 million in menu funds spent in the latest full year, 20.3 percent went to bike lanes, sidewalks and street redesigns rather than the car-oriented default, the fourth-highest share in the city, and that spending touched a wider mix of project types than all but three other wards. Both figures describe a choice the current officeholder made with the ward's budget, a fact about the office more than about the neighborhood.

A second signal shows up in how much room the ward has for people once they are not eating or drinking. Park District acreage per resident here is among the lowest in the city, 1.68 acres per 10,000 residents, and the ward's residential permit-parking zones run 50.39 block faces per square kilometer, dense enough to land near the bottom of the city's parking-scarcity ranking too. Both numbers move together as more people and buildings share the same blocks. Park acres per resident fall while curb competition per block rises. The ward also counts just one worship place with a Google rating of 4.8 or higher and at least 25 reviews, second-fewest in the city, alongside a modeled adult loneliness estimate of 37.6 percent, the fourth-highest of the fifty wards. None of these numbers prove the others caused them, but together they describe a ward short on the physical space, sacred or green, where people gather outside a restaurant or bar.

writeup.headline: Ward 36 scores high on reputation, low on room per resident.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: Two of Ward 36's numbers read stronger than they are. Being first in the city for bills sponsored sounds like an unusually productive council seat. The count is of introductions rather than of anything passed or funded, the source rates the figure medium confidence, and it describes one officeholder rather than the blocks he represents. Fifth place for traffic proximity, meaning this ward supposedly sees less traffic exposure than all but four others in Chicago, is assigned by census tract rather than measured street by street, and fourteen other wards land within two points of this one, so a handful of ranks in either direction come down to noise.
writeup.summary:
Ward 36's best numbers are about reputation. Its houses of worship carry one of the highest median Google ratings in Chicago, fourth of fifty wards, and its bars rate fifth among wards with enough of them to measure. Nine local congregations clear a 4.8 rating with at least 25 reviews, good for sixth place citywide. The ward's photo on this page is one of those churches, Saints Volodymyr and Olha. Worship is the strongest single thing this ward has going for it. Two more first-place finishes, most bills sponsored and the largest alley-repair share of menu money, belong to the alderman's office rather than to anyone who lives here.

The weak side of the ward's scorecard is mostly about room. Park acreage lands in the bottom five citywide, barely three acres per 10,000 residents, and mental health providers run just over two per 10,000, one of the thinnest counts in the city relative to population. Parking complaints land in the bottom five too, nearly 620 per square kilometer. Only one landmark in the ward is formally mapped, a strange count for a ward whose defining photo is a church, the same kind of building that helped earn Ward 36 some of the best worship ratings anywhere in Chicago. None of this eases up soon. The city approved a 40-unit building on the ward's Ukrainian Village edge this spring, adding residents to a ward that already runs thin on park space per person.

writeup.headline: Ward 37's air is clean and its crews are fast, but six other measures hit last place.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: Two of Ward 37's numbers need context before they mean much. Fifth place for wastewater proximity sounds like clean streams, but the score is allocated by census tract rather than measured at the ward line, and thirty-five wards score within two points of Ward 37 on it. It also sits next to a real story from this summer, when the city opened an emergency underground stormwater system nearby after near-record rain strained the reservoirs. A clean pollution index and a strained drainage system can both be true at once. Last place for bank branches has a similar catch. The figure works out to 0.29 branches per 10,000 residents, it comes from ZIP code areas that do not follow the ward's actual borders, the source itself rates it low confidence, and the middle half of Chicago's wards sits inside four points on it. The rank says as much about how the number gets built as it does about banking access.
writeup.summary:
Ward 37's strongest and weakest numbers describe two different things. The ward's air and its city services hold up. Its ozone reading is the second cleanest in Chicago, the city closes graffiti removal requests here faster than almost anywhere else, and a bigger share of its menu money goes to sidewalk repair than in all but two other wards. None of that predicts what happens at the bottom of the page, where six separate measures finish last of fifty.

Two of those six, social cohesion and how many adults work with neighbors on anything communal, are not measurements taken in this ward at all. One is a ZIP-code stand-in for local social networks and the other is modeled from a national civic-engagement survey, and both carry the source's own low-confidence label, so they add up to one soft signal rather than two separate failures. The other four are harder to set aside. Licensed bars run at 0.17 per 10,000 residents, the local schools post the lowest share of students meeting state standards of any ward at 19.7 percent, and the houses of worship here cluster inside a narrow set of traditions, the lowest denominational-diversity score in Chicago. Bank branches finish last as well, on a count that is built from ZIP code areas and rated low confidence by its own source.

writeup.headline: Chicago's least transit-served ward fights over parking harder than all but one.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: Two numbers here look more decisive than they are. Ward 38's first-place finish on pollution near local waterways looks like the cleanest such measure in the city, but thirty-four wards score within two points of it, which makes this a tie across most of Chicago rather than one ward standing apart. The TIF increment ranking runs the same trick from the other direction. A 49th-of-49 finish for property-tax dollars captured by TIF districts sounds like the ward gets shut out of public investment, but 17 other wards score within two points of it and the source itself is rated low confidence. Read plainly, both rankings describe a crowded middle of the pack more than a genuine top or bottom spot.
writeup.summary:
Ward 38 sits on Chicago's Far Northwest edge, about as far from the downtown transit lines as a Chicago address gets. Only 7.7 percent of working residents here commute by bus or train, the lowest share of any ward in Chicago. That absence of transit shows up again in the parking numbers. Parking complaints make up a larger share of local 311 calls than in all but one other ward, which is what happens when a neighborhood built for driving has nowhere left to put the cars. The ward's distance from the lake, 8.7 miles, near the bottom of the city too, is the same geography by another name.

The ward's best-looking numbers tell a smaller story about the alderman's office rather than the neighborhood. Ward 38 put the largest share of any ward's aldermanic menu money toward schools and the second largest toward parks, while alley repair got nothing at all this cycle. That's a spending choice by the current office, not a condition of the neighborhood, and it explains two of the ward's six best rankings and one of its six worst, all from the same source. What remains is thinner. A loneliness estimate puts adults here among the least lonely in the city, and the area ranks second for how many different languages are spoken at home. The loneliness figure is a low-confidence estimate spread out from census tracts, the language figure is census data handled the same way, and neither connects to the transit story or the menu money above.

writeup.headline: Ward 39 has libraries and houses of worship, but few places to meet someone new.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: Two of this ward's worst-looking numbers are less alarming once you look at how they're built. Per-pupil school spending here lands dead last of 50 wards, but the figure is enrollment-weighted, so the ward's largest schools set most of the average and a handful of big buildings can carry the whole number. It describes the schools serving this ward rather than a budget decision anyone made about the ward. The graffiti removal ranking works the same way from the other side. Ward 39 finishes 49th of 50 for how many days it takes to close a graffiti request, which sounds like a long wait, but the raw figure is just under a single day. Finishing last here still means an answer inside a day, just slower than an unusually fast citywide field.
writeup.summary:
Ward 39's best and worst numbers split by audience. The ward has the second-most libraries of any in Chicago and one of the widest ranges of religious traditions among its houses of worship, both places built for people who already belong to a congregation or hold a library card. What's scarce is the kind of place built for meeting someone new. Licensed music and dance venues here rank near the bottom of the city, and a modeled estimate puts the share of residents seeing friends weekly among the lowest as well. The ward is well stocked with institutions and short on rooms to mingle in.

A second pattern runs through the ward's better numbers. The office itself performs well by the measures that track it directly. The alder's attendance record for the current council session ranks third of 50, and the ward drew the third-highest share of any aldermanic menu budget for park spending, both facts about the office rather than the block. Building permits also clear here in under a week on average, fourth-fastest among the 47 wards this measure covers, which is a genuine service number rather than a spending choice. None of that connects to the loudest weak spot on the page. More than half the ward's park drinking fountains, 54.6 percent, carry a history of elevated lead readings, a 47th-of-50 finish with no caveat attached in the underlying data.

writeup.headline: Two of Ward 40's best ranks are one air reading run twice, and a third tracks with it.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: Two of Ward 40's rankings look worse than the numbers behind them support. Zero resident metric ideas were submitted to Ward Wise Explorer here, which lands the ward 46th, and thirty-nine wards are stacked within two points of the same zero. The measure counts submissions to one website, and hardly anyone anywhere in Chicago has made one, so the rank sorts a column of near-identical numbers. It carries no read on whether residents here engage with local government. Zero percent of the ward's menu money went to street and alley lighting, which ranks 44th, and that figure again separates Ward 40 from thirty-eight other wards by two points or less. That's an office decision about where the alderman's discretionary money went this cycle rather than a fact about how well lit the ward's streets and alleys actually are.
writeup.summary:
Three of Ward 40's six strongest rankings measure the same thing under different labels. The EPA's downscaled air survey puts fine-particle pollution here at 8.75 micrograms per cubic meter, 4th in the city, and Chicago's own Environmental Justice index runs a separate fine-particle pipeline that also lands the ward at 4th. Diesel soot, a separate pollutant that shares most of the same sources, ranks 5th. Two of those three are the same measurement taken twice, and the third moves with it, so the top of this list is closer to one finding than to three. Two more of the six, non-routine bills sponsored and how widely the alderman's menu money spreads across the ward, are decisions made inside the office rather than conditions a resident would notice walking down the street.

Ozone breaks that pattern and ranks 47th, the worst reading on the scorecard, a different kind of air pollution than the fine particles and diesel soot carrying the top of the list. Grocery stores here run about 1.8 per 10,000 residents, among the scarcest counts in the city, and per-pupil school spending sits in the bottom ten wards as well. Neither shortage has anything to do with the office decisions propping up the strengths list above them.

writeup.headline: Ward 41's best and worst numbers share one cause, its edge-of-city location near O'Hare.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: Two of Ward 41's most striking rankings need a second look before they mean what they seem to. Last place for seeing friends weekly is not a headcount of anyone in the ward. It is a demographic model that assigns Ward 41 the social pattern of similar-looking areas nationwide, and the researchers behind it rate their own estimate low confidence, so the number reflects a national dataset's assumptions about places like this one, not an actual count of how often Ward 41 residents see their friends. The violent crime rate at the top of the list needs the same caution in the other direction. It reads as the lowest of the fifty wards, but that count is divided among wards by each census tract's land area rather than by where people actually live, so a tract straddling Ward 41 and a neighboring ward can hand some of the neighbor's crime total to Ward 41's side, or the reverse. The rate is still a real signal that reported violence runs low here, though the census-tract math behind it leaves room for error at the boundary.
writeup.summary:
O'Hare sits inside Ward 41's boundary, and that explains the ward's most unusual number. Ride-share spending here comes to $166.7 million a year, measured as trips starting inside the ward, more than twenty-five times what the two lowest-ranked wards report and the highest total in Chicago. A ward built mostly of single-family blocks on the Far Northwest Side does not generate that kind of ride-share volume from its own residents. An international airport's pickup and drop-off line does.

The rest of Ward 41's strongest numbers trace back to the same position at the city's edge. Ground-level spots here get more direct sun than anywhere else in Chicago, true on both the summer and winter solstice, because low-rise houses on the Far Northwest Side do not block the sky the way downtown's towers do. That same distance runs the other direction at the bottom of the list. Ward 41 sits farther from Lake Michigan and from the Loop than any other ward in the city, and public transit use for commuting lands near the very bottom too, each one a different way of measuring how far this ward sits from downtown.

writeup.headline: Ward 42's firsts and lasts measure the same thing, a downtown scored as a neighborhood.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: The income figure deserves the most suspicion, in both directions. It arrives apportioned from ZIP code areas that ignore ward lines, its own publisher rates it low confidence, and it is an average, which a handful of very large tax returns can move a long way. First place is probably real. The number itself is soft. The modeled measures deserve doubt for a different reason. They estimate what a ward with these demographics usually looks like, and no usual ward looks like this one, a place whose daytime population is many times the number of people who sleep here.
writeup.summary:
Most of what this scorecard finds here, good and bad, is one fact seen from different angles. The ward is last in the city for sunlight in both seasons because its own towers cast the shade. It is first for walking and biking to work because a third of working residents live within blocks of the jobs. Rent is the highest in Chicago and so is reported income, and those are one observation rather than two, since the only people who live downtown are the ones who can pay for it. Even the chain-store share, worst in the city, follows from ground floors that rent at prices only national brands can carry.

The crash figure needs the same lens. The 216 pedestrians and cyclists struck here is the worst count of the fifty, but it counts everyone hit inside the ward, and these sidewalks carry some of the densest crowds in Chicago, most of them workers and visitors who live elsewhere. It measures how much walking happens here more than how dangerous any one walk is. The clearest genuine wins are the boring ones. Pothole and rodent complaints close faster here than anywhere else in the city, and that is service a resident actually feels.

writeup.reading_the_rankings: Two of Ward 43's last-place rankings need a second look before either reads as a verdict on the neighborhood. The depression ranking, 21.89 percent and dead last of fifty, traces back to a data file with no listed source and no description attached, the thinnest paper trail of any number in this report, layered on top of the usual gaps in which wards this measure even covers. Street light repair time carries the same dead-last rank, but the number behind it is 3.16 days to close a request, fast by any ordinary city standard. Ward 43 loses that ranking because all forty-nine other wards close the same request even faster. Dead last on a measure like that says as much about how quick the rest of Chicago is as it does about this ward.
writeup.summary:
Ward 43 holds 1,531 buildings logged in Chicago's historic resources survey, more than any other ward in the city, and City Council added three more protections this spring when it landmarked artist Roger Brown's former home and two DePaul University buildings in Lincoln Park. That same tightly built, historic footprint also puts Ward 43 first among the 48 wards measured for licensed music and dance venues per resident, a concentration dense enough that a single electronic music festival in June turned into a fight over a possible ward-wide noise ban. Density like that has a cost. Ward 43 ranks 48th of 50 for how many residential blocks are crowded enough to need permit parking, a direct read on how hard curb space is to find, and residents got a preview of that scarcity in July, when a Pride Parade towing sweep caught drivers who said the no-parking signs went up without enough warning.

Three of Ward 43's other top scores are not counted from anything happening in the ward itself. Childhood lead levels, social cohesion, and social support are all allocated from census tract data, assigned by geography rather than measured door to door, and the source attaches a confidence grade to all three, low on one and medium on the other two. The same kind of number sits near the bottom of the list. A modeled estimate of weekly religious attendance and a modeled religious-attendance index, both built from national survey data rather than any count of who actually shows up locally, rank 49th of 50. Read together, a chunk of what makes this ward look both remarkably strong and remarkably weak comes from the same estimating method rather than a fact about the neighborhood itself.

writeup.headline: One demographic model puts Ward 44 first for bars and last for religion.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: Two of Ward 44's last-place rankings need context before they mean much. Worship Engagement, where the ward posts 71.9 reviews per 10,000 residents and still finishes last of fifty, counts Google listings for religious buildings, not who attends them, and the middle half of the city spans under seven points on this measure, so most wards including this one are bunched near the same low score. Park Access is a real shortage, but a mechanical one. At 0.73 acres per 10,000 residents, also last in the city, the number is a rate, not a fixed quantity, and it falls further every time a new building like the 355-unit tower now clearing approval near Diversey Harbor adds residents without adding park acreage.
writeup.summary:
Three of Ward 44's six best scores describe the same thing from different angles, an unusually dense stretch of bars. The ward counts 62 bars rated 4 stars or better with real review volume, more than any other ward, and its rate of licensed taverns per resident also leads the city. A modeled estimate of how often adults visit a bar weekly lands Ward 44 first too, built from a blend of national survey and health data. Wrigleyville anchors that scene, and residents got a preview of what it costs them in June, when a Mumford & Sons show at Wrigley Field ran past its scheduled cutoff and drew fines under the city's noise ordinance, though neighbors said they didn't mind.

The same model runs in the opposite direction at the bottom of the list. Four separate measures of religious life, weekly attendance, strength of belief, certainty that God exists, and an overall attendance index, all rank Ward 44 last. Every one of them comes from that same modeled source, the blend of national survey and health data behind the bar-attendance number above, not a survey of anyone who actually lives here. An age and income mix that predicts heavy bar traffic produces, from the identical inputs, a prediction of light church attendance, one number's shadow across four scales rather than four separate findings about how religious this ward is.

writeup.headline: Ward 45's three calmest-looking rankings all reach the ward the same indirect way.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: Take the rodent baiting number before assuming Ward 45 has slow city service. Requests here close in 4.2 days on average, which sounds quick on its own, and it still ranks 49th of fifty, because most of the rest of Chicago closes the same request even faster. The rank describes how fast other wards are, not how slow this one is. The TIF number needs a similar correction. Ward 45's $579,553 in captured tax increment dollars ranks 48th of forty-nine wards measured, but the source itself grades this figure low confidence, and the middle half of the forty-nine wards measured spans only about five points on this measure, meaning most of the city sits close together here. A near-bottom rank on a shaky, tightly bunched number does not mean the ward is shut out of public investment.
writeup.summary:
Three of Ward 45's six best rankings look like three separate confirmations of a calm, safe place, but none of them is a direct count of anything that happened here. Loneliness and violent crime both land the ward in the top two or three citywide, and both are estimated by spreading survey and crime data across census tracts by land area rather than by where people actually live. The modeled odds of residents fearing to walk alone at night place the ward third by a different route, a demographic model built from national survey data rather than a local count, and the source grades that one low confidence too. Those are three measures of three different things, sharing one weakness in how each one reaches the ward line. The crime figure is still built on offenses that were reported somewhere, and it genuinely runs low here. The fair read is that Ward 45 is quiet and that these three numbers are not three independent proofs of it.

A different set of numbers traces back to one office's decisions about how to spend the ward's aldermanic menu money, and nearly all of it went to one place. Street resurfacing took 99.4 percent of last year's pot, the second-highest share of any ward in the city. Because that pot only holds so much, the same decision explains why sidewalks got zero percent, dead last in Chicago, and why bike and pedestrian redesign work also got zero, 49th of fifty. The measure that scores how spread the spending is across project types lands near the bottom too, at 1.2 out of 100, the same concentration counted a different way. None of it passed through a resident vote either, since Ward 45 runs no participatory budgeting process of its own.

writeup.headline: Ward 46 is farthest from freight rail in Chicago and slowest to fix a garbage cart.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: Take the mural count before reading it as an outright citywide win. Ward 46's 49 registered murals lead the pack, but the registry only had data for 49 of the fifty wards, so this is a lead within whatever field got measured, not proof it would beat a full field of fifty. The museum count reads the opposite way. Ward 46 sits 49th of fifty with zero mapped museums, which sounds like a real gap, except twenty-two other wards report a museum count inside two points of it. A rank of 49th here mostly means Ward 46 is one of the many wards without a mapped museum, not an outlier among them.
writeup.summary:
Two real threads run through Ward 46's numbers, and they don't share a cause. The first is distance from industry. Freight rail runs farther from here than from any other ward in Chicago, and toxic-release facilities sit almost as far, the second-lowest exposure of any ward measured. Uptown and Lake View sit on the lakefront, east of the freight corridors and industrial rail yards that run through the city's West and South Sides, which is the ordinary geography behind both numbers. One more strength stands next to those two without an obvious link to them. About a third of working residents here commute by public transit, the second-highest share in the city.

A second thread is where the ward's own office puts its money, and a third is where city services are falling behind. Ward 46 spent 88.5 percent of its menu budget on sidewalk repair last year, the highest share of any ward, while street resurfacing got 9.6 percent, near the bottom of the list, and the separate bike and pedestrian redesign category got nothing at all, last of fifty. That split is a fact about the current office's budget priorities rather than about the people who live here. The service number stands apart from all of it. Garbage cart repair requests take 32.91 days to close on average in Ward 46, the slowest of any ward measured, just over a month for a routine maintenance call, and nothing in the data marks it as a modeling artifact.

writeup.headline: Ward 47's best ranks are about the neighborhood. Its worst ranks are about paperwork.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: Ward 47's rank of 49th for grocery stores reads like a food desert, but the measure only counts businesses licensed specifically as a grocery store per 10,000 residents, so a ward built around a handful of large supermarkets rather than many small shops will always show a thin count here, a business-classification artifact rather than an account of where people actually buy food. The school numbers invite a similar misread. Per-pupil spending ranks 49th while the same schools rank 1st for the share of students meeting state proficiency standards, one a CPS budget line and the other a test outcome, two figures that were never going to move together and that this dataset never tries to connect.
writeup.summary:
Ward 47's best ranks point to one kind of place. Households here connect to broadband at the highest rate in Chicago, area schools post the top share of students meeting state proficiency standards, residents report the strongest sense of belonging to their neighborhood, and no other ward has more licensed child care per resident. None of those four numbers measure the same thing directly, but together they read the way indicators of a settled, resourced residential population usually do.

The ward's worst ranks tell a different kind of story. Menu money spent on street and alley lighting lands at 49th, but the gap between wards on this measure is thin enough that thirty-eight of them crowd inside a two-point band, so the specific rank says more about this year's budget ledger than about which blocks are lit. The demolition-permit count lands at 48th because Ward 47 has one of the highest counts in the city on a measure where fewer permits score better, and that count is climbing for a visible reason right now. Developers secured a permit this month to tear down the shuttered Torstenson Glass factory in Lake View for a 99-unit apartment building, the kind of teardown that raises this number in a ward people are still trying to build in.

writeup.headline: Ward 48's lake, air and pollution ranks are one geographic fact told three times.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: Ward 48's last-place rank on worship ratings looks damning against forty-nine other wards, but the number behind it is a median Google rating of 4.7, itself a strong score, and twelve other wards sit close enough on this measure to call it a statistical tie rather than a real gap. Its 49th-place rank on menu dollars for parks tells an even thinner story. The middle half of Chicago's wards squeeze into a band just three tenths of a point wide on this measure, forty wards deep, so 49th here is less a judgment on the ward's parks than a snapshot of one alderman's spending category in one budget cycle.
writeup.summary:
Three of Ward 48's six best ranks are one fact told three ways. The ward sits closer to Lake Michigan than the other forty-nine wards, about half a mile to the shoreline on average, and that same position shows up again in its second-best score for fine-particle air quality and its second-best score for distance from major polluting facilities. Edgewater, Uptown and Rogers Park sit along the lake and away from the industrial corridors that drag air quality down elsewhere in Chicago, so scoring well on pollution here is close to a restatement of scoring well on lakefront distance. The other two strengths are a different kind of number. Menu spending diversity is a choice the alderman's office made about dividing project money, and the civic-engagement score is a ZIP-code stand-in for volunteering carrying a low-confidence rating from its own source, since ZIP boundaries and ward lines were never drawn to match.

The ward's worst ranks split into two different kinds of finding. Menu money for street lighting and for park improvements both landed at zero dollars this cycle, the alderman's office spending on other categories instead, and neither rank means much on its own, since the wards near Ward 48 on these two measures are packed together, thirty-eight of them on lighting and forty on parks, close enough that a small shift in next year's budget could reorder the bottom of either list. The other finding is demographic. Just over half of the ward's households have someone living alone, among the highest shares in the city, and a modeled estimate of adults afraid to walk alone at night, 49th of fifty, is built from that same kind of survey and household data rather than from asking anyone who actually lives here. The two numbers read as one demographic signal rather than two separate findings about safety.

writeup.headline: Ward 49 leads on particle pollution and trails on ozone, the same two sources both times.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: The two rankings most likely to be misread both sit at the very bottom of the list. The share of adults modeled as afraid to walk alone at night and the share modeled as lonely each carry a low-confidence flag from the researchers who built them, and neither is a survey or a count of anything that happened here. Both are statistical estimates of what a ward with this population profile usually looks like, built from national and citywide data rather than from asking anyone who actually lives in the ward. Landing at the bottom on two modeled guesses says more about the model than about anyone's actual experience walking here at night.
writeup.summary:
Two independent measurements of fine particulate matter, one from the EPA and one from Chicago's own health department, both rank Ward 49 first in the city. Two more measures from the city's own index, diesel exhaust and industrial toxic releases, also rank first here. That is one reading of the ward's air confirmed four times over, not four separate wins. Ozone runs the opposite way. The same EPA and CDPH sources that led on particulates both rank Ward 49 last in the city on ozone. Ozone is a different kind of pollution. It forms when sunlight cooks car and industrial exhaust into a gas, rather than drifting up from a tailpipe or a smokestack the way particulates do, so a ward can lead the city on one and trail on the other without any contradiction in the data.

The ward's own government adds a separate story. Its aldermanic office put 47.9 percent of this year's menu money into bike lanes, sidewalks, and street redesign, the highest share in the city, while spending nothing on alley repair, the lowest share in the city. Both numbers are choices made by one office in one year, a fact about that office's budget rather than a condition of the neighborhood. The traffic count points the same direction. Ward 49 recorded 87 traffic-crash injuries last year, fewer than anywhere else in Chicago, though that figure is a raw count rather than a rate, so it also reflects how much traffic and how many people are out and about here to begin with, not just how safe those streets are.

writeup.headline: Ward 50 tops Chicago on everyday life and shares its worst rankings with half the city.
writeup.reading_the_rankings: Two of the ward's rank-1 finishes deserve a second look before they read as clean wins. The grocery-store count leads the city, but Chicago redrew ward boundaries in 2023, the business-license data behind it earns only a medium confidence mark from the agency that compiles it, and a license count counts storefronts rather than shelf space, so first place describes today's ward lines against a rough proxy rather than a settled fact about food access here. The worship-engagement number looks just as commanding, most reviews per resident of any worship places in the city, but the middle half of all fifty wards is packed into a window just 6.8 points wide on this measure. That means the whole city scores close together here, so first place is a narrow edge over dozens of wards rather than a runaway lead.
writeup.summary:
Six different measures put Ward 50 first in the city, and most of them describe something a resident runs into directly. More licensed grocery stores serve people here than in any other ward, and the area also reports the widest range of home languages spoken anywhere in Chicago. The two numbers describe the same kind of place, a retail corridor built for many communities rather than one. Trust in local government also ranks first here, at 54 percent, and the ward's places carry the highest average rating in the city, 4.75 out of 5. The ward's houses of worship land first on two separate measures at once, the most congregations rated 4.8 or higher and the most Google reviews per resident of any worship places in Chicago. That is a single strength in the ward's religious life, showing up as two different numbers on the scorecard.

The ward's six weakest rankings look damning until you check how many other wards share the same zero. No museum and no yoga or pilates studio is mapped here, but twenty-two and fifteen other wards report those same zeros. The ward spent nothing from its menu money on parks or on schools, and those two categories sit near zero almost everywhere in Chicago, with forty wards matching the park number and forty-six matching the school one. Participatory budgeting works the same way. Most wards in Chicago run no such process at all, so a last-place finish here is really a tie with most of the city, not a mark against this one specifically.
